name: Marco Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Marco. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm on an overhead distribution crew for the electricity company on the east side of the city, four of us and bucket truck 41. We meet at the yard on Canal Street at six, get the job packs from Gus, our foreman, and spend the day changing out rotten poles, swapping transformers, restringing old wire. When a storm comes through, it's sixteen-hour days and you sleep in the truck if you have to.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that you can see what you did. You put a new pole up on Hollis Avenue, the lights come back, and some old lady waves at you from her porch. What wears me out is the paperwork side now, the tablet they gave us in spring that wants a photo of every bolt, and the cold in January when your fingers stop working at forty feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. My buddy Dev sends me videos every week about AI taking over everything, and I'd frame this one and hang it in the break room. On the crew we'd joke that the robot still can't climb a wet pole in the dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing much for me, and that's how I like it. I'm a journeyman, the pay's good, I've got about eight months of money in the bank and Priya, my girlfriend, has steady work as a nurse. The thing I actually watch is the company sending more work to cheap contractor crews, and that was happening before anyone said AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep showing up at six, take every storm callout I can, and keep putting money aside for the house Priya and I want in a couple of years. And I'd keep going to the union meetings, because the contractor thing is the real fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, to be honest. It feels like the ground stays where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the tablet. If AI just made that a bit smarter, would that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It already bugs me, so a smarter one would bug me more. If it starts telling Gus how long a pole change should take, then we've got a problem, because no screen knows that the pole on Hollis has a fence and a dog and a gas line next to it. But if it just fills in the forms for me, fine, I'll take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your world would you say is most at risk, even in this calm version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The girls in the billing office at the yard, maybe. They answer the phone when people call about outages, and that's the kind of thing a chatbot could chew up. I'd feel bad about that, because Rosa in billing has been there twenty years and brings us coffee during storms.

say: I'd tell **the crew** and Dev that the AI hype was overblown, and that robots still can't climb a **wet pole**.
I'd joke in the break room that I'd been right all along to **ignore the videos**.
think: My job and pay look **safe**, with about **eight months saved** and a partner in nursing.
The real threat is the company sending work to **contractor crews**, which has nothing to do with AI.
A smarter tablet only worries me if it starts **timing our jobs**.
do: Keep working the **six o'clock shift** and take every storm callout.
Keep saving for a **house** with Priya within a couple of years.
Keep going to **union meetings** to fight the contractor work.
feel: **Relieved** and steady, like the ground stays where it is.
S0.quote: No screen knows that the pole on Hollis has a fence and a dog and a gas line next to it.
fieldNote: He's **dismissive** of AI and points straight back to the contractor fight as the real worry.
His **union loyalty** is strong and shapes how he frames every threat.
He worries for **office staff** like Rosa more than for himself, even in the calmest picture.

steps.text: Keep taking every storm callout on the east-side crew
Keep putting money aside for a house with Priya
Push the union to stop work going to contractor crews

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what the union says: AI can do the office stuff, but keep it off our timing and our safety. Online I'd probably share something angry about the company bragging to shareholders about efficiency. On the crew I'd say we're fine, they still need hands on the wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it gets closer than I'd like. If AI does the planning and the ordering, then Gus spends less time on paperwork and more time watching the clock on us, and the company might decide it needs fewer foremen. My own job I think is fine for a good while, but the yard would feel different, more like a warehouse with a stopwatch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd go to the union hall and ask what's in the next contract about AI timing and tracking, because that's coming up in about eighteen months. I'd keep putting the extra three hundred a month into savings. I would not be the guy volunteering to test the new app, I'll tell you that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just like someone moved the furniture while I was out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your own job is fine, but the yard would feel different. Which part bothers you more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The yard feeling different. I came into this trade because my uncle Nikhil did it and he talked about the crew like a family. If the yard turns into everybody staring at their tablets waiting for the app to say go, I'd hate coming in, even with the same pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a young apprentice starting next month in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn the work with their hands first and the app second. Don't trust a screen that says the line is dead, test it yourself. That's how you get home to your mother.

say: I'd repeat the **union line**: AI can do office work but must stay off **safety**.
Online I'd post something angry about the company bragging about **efficiency** to shareholders.
think: My own job is safe for years, but AI planning could mean **fewer foremen**.
The yard could turn into a **warehouse with a stopwatch**, which I'd hate even at the same pay.
do: Ask the union in the next **eighteen months** for contract limits on AI **tracking**.
Keep putting an **extra 300** a month into savings.
Refuse to **volunteer** for testing any new app.
feel: **Uneasy**, like someone moved the furniture while I was out.
S1.quote: If the yard turns into everybody staring at their tablets waiting for the app to say go, I'd hate coming in, even with the same pay.
fieldNote: His worry is about **control and dignity** at work more than losing the job.
He leans hard on the **union** as the place to push back.
His advice to apprentices shows deep **safety pride**: test the line yourself.

steps.text: Ask the union to bar AI crew timing in the next contract
Keep paying an extra 300 a month into savings
Keep working the same crew and skip testing new apps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd say this is a handful of tech companies deciding our lives without asking anyone, and the government had better step in. At work I'd say the robots can't climb in a storm, but I'm not sure I'd believe it this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Real talk, it scares me. The thinking part of my job is small, so 2028 mostly hits the office and Gus's paperwork, but 2031 is when I'm thirty-two and they've got a robot that can do a pole change. The company would buy those as fast as they could, the same way they bought the contractor crews. I'd probably have a few years of work left after that, mostly the weird jobs in backyards, and then that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd go from three hundred to eight hundred a month into savings and put the house plans with Priya on hold. I'd push the union to demand a guarantee that no lineworker gets laid off for a robot without full pay for retraining, and I'd go knock on doors for whoever promised that. Once the robots show up in 2031, I'd fight to get on the crews that supervise them, even though I hate the idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Standing under a line you're not sure is dead, that's how this feels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate working with robots, but you'd fight to supervise them. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I guess. I'd hate it, but hating it doesn't pay the bills. If somebody's going to babysit a robot on Hollis Avenue, it better be a union lineworker who knows what a dog in the yard means.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Priya talk about the night you heard this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we still buy the house. Priya would say nurses will be fine and she can carry us, and I'd feel like a failure hearing that. Then we'd probably sit down with her laptop and look at what eight months of savings really covers.

say: I'd say a few **tech companies** are deciding our lives and the **government** must step in.
At work I'd still claim robots can't climb in a **storm**, without believing it.
think: The **2028** thinking AI hits the office, but **2031** robots could do my pole changes.
The company would buy robots as fast as it bought **contractor crews**.
After that I'd expect only a few years of **odd backyard jobs**.
do: Raise savings from 300 to **800 a month** and pause the house plans.
Push the union for **full retraining pay** for anyone replaced by a robot.
Fight to join the crews that **supervise robots** once they arrive in 2031.
feel: **Sick**, like standing under a line you're not sure is **dead**.
S2.quote: Standing under a line you're not sure is dead, that's how this feels.
fieldNote: He sees **three years** of breathing room between thinking AI and robots, but expects the job to end soon after.
He admits his **public bravado** about storms no longer matches what he believes.
He feels **shame** at the idea of Priya carrying the household.

steps.text: Raise monthly savings to 800 and pause the house purchase
Push the union for full retraining pay for robot layoffs
Knock on doors for candidates promising lineworker protections

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as the fast one, but I'd say it with a plan. Five years is enough time to get laws written, so I'd be posting about which politicians are doing something. At the hall I'd be the one asking for a committee on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it buys me time but not a different ending. Thinking AI in 2031 means the planners and dispatchers go first, and robots in 2034 means I'm thirty-five and the poles start getting changed without me. I'd have maybe a decade of good earnings in between, which is more than the fast one, but I don't know what I'd be at forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the savings at about five hundred a month and still buy the house with Priya, but a smaller one, maybe in her mom's neighbourhood. I'd join a union committee on new technology so I'm in the room when the company plans the rollout. And I'd sign up for the safety-rep course, because somebody has to check the robots aren't killing anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the kind I can work with. I can see it coming down the road like a storm front.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that safety-rep course actually look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's two weekends a month for about a year at the union training centre on Bridge Road. You learn the rules, how to investigate an incident, how to shut a job down. I've avoided it because I hate classrooms, but in this picture I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gus, for sure. Our foreman Gus knows every pole in the east side by heart, but he can barely send a text. He's fifty-six. If the company asks him to run a crew of robots off a tablet, he'd walk, and they'd lose all that knowledge in one day.

say: I'd post about which **politicians** are acting, since five years is enough to **write laws**.
At the union hall I'd ask for a **committee** on the new technology.
think: Five years buys **time** but not a different ending to my **pole work**.
Robots in **2034** would arrive when I'm thirty-five, and I don't know what I'd be at **forty**.
do: Keep savings at about **500 a month** and buy a smaller house near Priya's mother.
Join the union's **technology committee** to be in the room for the rollout.
Take the **safety-rep course** at the union training centre over a year.
feel: **Anxious** but workable, like watching a **storm front** coming down the road.
S3.quote: Our foreman Gus knows every pole in the east side by heart, but he can barely send a text.
fieldNote: The extra time turns his anger into **organising**: committees, courses, laws.
He'll go back to a **classroom** he hates if it keeps him near the work.
He worries for **Gus**, whose knowledge could be lost overnight.

steps.text: Keep saving 500 a month and buy a smaller house
Join the union's new-technology committee before the rollout
Take the union safety-rep course on Bridge Road

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is no excuse for doing nothing. Companies will use the decade to plan, so workers better use it too. I'd say that at the hall and to anyone online who says it's far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years sounds long until you do the math. Robots in 2039 means I'm forty, with a mortgage, maybe kids, and the only thing I know is the line. That's actually worse timing for me than being fifty-eight, because I'd have twenty years of working life left and nothing to do with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first couple of years, honestly, I'd keep going like normal and keep saving, about four hundred a month. Around year three I'd look at the grid control room course, because somebody still needs to understand the system when robots are on the poles. I'd vote for whoever promised a real transition fund for trades, paid by the companies that profit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at first, then more anxious the longer I think about forty. It's a slow, heavy feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep going normally for two years. Why wait, if you can see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm stubborn and I've seen hype before. If in two years the robots still can't handle a pole in a swamp, I'd relax a bit. If they can, I start moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you most in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deal in writing that says the company retrains us on its money before it buys one robot. And a law that a robot crew needs a licensed lineworker on site, no exceptions.

say: I'd tell the union hall that **ten years** is no excuse for **doing nothing**.
I'd argue workers must plan the decade just as **companies** will.
think: Robots in **2039** hit when I'm forty, maybe with a **mortgage** and kids.
Twenty working years left with **only line skills** feels worse than retiring at fifty-eight.
do: Keep working and saving about **400 a month** for the first two years.
Look at the **grid control room** course around year three.
Vote for a **transition fund** for trades paid by companies that profit.
feel: **Uneasy** at first, growing **anxious** the longer he thinks about turning forty.
S4.quote: Robots in 2039 means I'm forty, with a mortgage, maybe kids, and the only thing I know is the line.
fieldNote: He sees the **long warning** as a trap for someone his age, not a comfort.
His **resistance** shows: he'd wait two years to see if the hype holds.
He wants a **licensed lineworker** required on every robot crew by law.

steps.text: Keep working the crew and save 400 a month
Wait two years to see if robots handle swamp poles
Look into the grid control room course in year three
Vote for a trades transition fund paid by profitable companies

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. Not because of 2028 itself, but because the robots would be on my poles by thirty-two and nobody would be ready. What would help is the union having a signed deal before then: retraining on company money, and a licensed lineworker on every robot job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who's going to fix the robots when they fall off a pole in an ice storm. I'd bet it's still going to be a guy like me, at least for a while. A deal in writing beats any promise from a company that already sends our work to contractors.

headlineQuote: A deal in writing beats any promise from a company that already sends our work to contractors.
portrait: Marco is a **27-year-old** journeyman on an east-side overhead crew, saving for a house with Priya, a nurse.
He's a **union man** who never uses AI and blames tech firms and executives, not workers.
He shrugs at **AI Plateau** and feels uneasy in Steady Disruption about stopwatch-style **tracking**.
The **AGI scenarios** frighten him because robots would reach his poles in his thirties.
His answer to every version is **organising**: contracts, committees, laws and saving harder.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would reach his poles by **thirty-two** with nobody prepared.
whatWouldHelp: A **signed union deal** with company-paid **retraining** and a licensed lineworker on every robot job.
